metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.method: Manual inspection of the reusable Swift micro (mb00-mb11) and adversarial (ADV-*) programs under template/programs/swift, scored per language_quality.md guidance: idiomatic, production-reasonable Swift, no artificial verbosity or artificial brevity.
observations: Swift core constructs (struct value types with mutating funcs, trailing-closure syntax, string interpolation, range operators, guard/if-let optional binding) let algorithmic logic (mb01 fib, mb04 accumulator loop, mb10 buffered IO/parsing) be expressed compactly without extra helper boilerplate.

Some structural overhead is intrinsic to the language/runtime rather than to workload authoring: conditional import Darwin/Glibc for fflush, mandatory do/try/catch around every Foundation FileHandle call in mb10, and the CommandLine.arguments plus ContinuousClock harness repeated in every micro file, required uniformly by the frozen benchmark harness and not Swift-specific bloat.

Swift standard library has no first-class buffered line writer/reader, only Foundation FileHandle primitives, so mb10 manual 65536-byte buffer flush/read/carry-over loop is longer than the buffered-IO idioms available out of the box in some comparison languages such as Java BufferedWriter/Reader or Go bufio, a real conciseness cost attributable to language/stdlib design.

Type inference reduces line noise versus explicitly-typed languages; no unnecessary copies observed, mb04 indexes arrays directly and mb10 uses ArraySlice UInt8 to avoid copying buffer subranges, consistent with fair non-penalizing idiom usage.
metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.score_rationale: 78 of 100: strong conciseness from modern syntax offset by mandatory error-handling ceremony on every Foundation IO call and the stdlib lack of built-in buffered or streaming IO, forcing longer manual implementations for IO-heavy workloads than several comparison languages achieve idiomatically.

metric.readability.method: Manual review of naming, control flow, structuring, and commenting conventions across the same Swift micro and adversarial corpus.
observations: Consistent descriptive naming such as workload, main, parseDecimal, splitLine, Lcg and doc comments on structs and functions aid readability, reflecting normal idiomatic Swift style, not benchmark-specific dressing.

guard-let and optional binding patterns make error and failure paths locally visible and linear rather than deeply nested, a genuine Swift language-design readability strength versus languages requiring nested null checks.
Trailing closure syntax and structured timing APIs such as ContinuousClock read naturally in-line without extra ceremony.

Some readability friction: low-level byte-level parsing required for the frozen IO buffer contract is inherently less readable than string-level APIs, though this constraint is applied identically across languages, not Swift-specific.
mutating func and value-type struct semantics are explicitly marked, aiding reasoning about state mutation compared to languages where mutation is implicit.
metric.readability.score_rationale: 84 of 100: Swift optional-binding control flow, strong static typing with inference, and doc-comment conventions yield high readability; minor deductions for byte-level Foundation API verbosity required by IO-heavy workloads and the necessity of explicit do-catch blocks around routine IO.
